evals.name: pc-cookie-dough
evals.prompt: I run a small bakery facility registered with FDA. We're adding a refrigerated ready-to-bake chocolate chip cookie dough with walnuts, sold in retail tubs. Ingredients: heat-treated flour from a supplier, liquid pasteurized eggs, butter, sugar, chocolate chips, walnuts. We mix, deposit into tubs, label and ship refrigerated. Do a hazard analysis for this under the FSMA Preventive Controls for Human Food rule and tell me which preventive controls I need.
assertions: Uses the hazard analysis structure: steps and ingredients, identify biological/chemical/physical hazards, decide whether each requires a preventive control, and justify each decision
Considers foreseeable use: consumers eating the dough raw, so pathogens in flour (E. coli/Salmonella) are a hazard needing control
Identifies a supply-chain preventive control for the supplier-applied heat treatment of flour (and/or pasteurized eggs), since there is no kill step in the facility
Identifies food allergen controls for milk, egg, wheat, tree nuts (walnut) and soy if present: labeling control and cross-contact controls
Identifies a process control for refrigeration/temperature (time-temperature) or notes the environmental pathogen hazard for exposed RTE product with sanitation control and environmental monitoring
States a recall plan is required because hazards requiring preventive controls were identified

evals.name: pc-supplier-audit
evals.prompt: We buy pasteurized liquid egg from one supplier and use it in a ready-to-eat product with no further cook. Our QA lead wants to just accept the supplier's own annual self-audit and a certificate of analysis. Is that enough under the FSMA PCHF rule? What does our supply-chain program actually have to include?
assertions: States that Salmonella in eggs is a hazard that can cause serious adverse health consequences or death (SAHCODHA)
States that for a SAHCODHA hazard the default verification is an onsite audit before using the supplier and at least annually, unless there is a written justification for other activities
States that a supplier's self-audit is not acceptable as supplier verification
Explains a COA can support verification but is not a substitute for the required onsite audit by a qualified auditor
Lists supply-chain program elements: approved suppliers, written receiving procedures, determining and conducting verification activities, corrective action, records
Mentions the onsite audit must be done by a qualified auditor (can be third party)

evals.name: pc-cook-deviation
evals.prompt: Our cook step is a process preventive control with a critical limit of product surface temperature at or above 158 F. This morning the operator measured 152 F on one batch and it had already been moved to assembly. Walk me through what we have to do, the difference between a correction and a corrective action, and what verification and record timelines apply under 21 CFR 117.
assertions: Says this is a deviation from a critical limit requiring a corrective action (not merely a correction)
Lists corrective action elements: identify and correct the problem, reduce likelihood of recurrence, evaluate affected food for safety, prevent adulterated food entering commerce, document it
Defines a correction as a prompt action for a minor, isolated problem that does not directly affect product safety, with less documentation
States monitoring and corrective action records must be reviewed by (or under oversight of) a PCQI within 7 working days
States validation of process controls is required (within 90 days of production or before implementation) and mentions calibration of the thermometer
States records must be kept at least 2 years, and mentions reanalysis if controls are found ineffective
